The prototype as the new specification

When building is cheap, the working artefact can carry most of the decision — but only the decisions it makes visible. Everything else has to be written down, and knowing which is which is the whole skill.

1. A Tuesday in Bengaluru

On Tuesday 14 October 2025, eleven days before Diwali, Meera Raghunathan sat in a glass room on the fourth floor of Baithak Systems' office off Bannerghatta Road with two laptops open in front of her. Baithak sells scheduling and dispatch software to the after-sales service networks of large appliance and electronics brands: when a customer's washing machine fails in Coimbatore, Baithak's software decides which technician goes, when, carrying which part. Baithak's software touches about 4.2 lakh jobs a month across eleven service networks, and its largest contract, worth ₹3.4 crore a year, carries a service-level agreement that penalises the company if dispatch decisions take longer than four seconds at peak.

On the left-hand laptop was a nine-page prose document: a product requirements document, or PRD — the traditional written artefact in which a product manager states what is to be built and why. On the right-hand laptop was a working web application. Rohit Deshmukh, a product manager two years into the job, had built it over the previous weekend using an AI coding assistant. It ran in a browser, it had a technician roster, a map, a drag-and-drop queue, and an "auto-dispatch" button that actually assigned jobs. It had taken him about eleven hours. The PRD, written by Meera's team the previous quarter for a comparable feature, had taken twenty-four hours of writing and two rounds of review over nine days.

Kaushik Iyer, who leads the four-person engineering team in Pune, had seen the prototype on Monday evening and sent a single line on Slack at 11:40 p.m.: "This is lovely. It is not a spec. What happens when two dispatchers hit auto-assign on the same job at the same time?" Meera had to decide by Thursday what the team would build against during the Diwali-to-January window — the prototype, the prose, or something she had not yet named. If she chose wrong in the direction of prose, she would burn three weeks of a nine-week window re-arguing decisions the prototype had already settled. If she chose wrong in the direction of the prototype, the team would ship something that looked exactly like the demo and fell over the first time a Reliance-scale service network pushed 900 concurrent jobs through it during the festive-season rush.

2. The idea, stated precisely

The claim behind "the prototype as the new specification" is narrow and worth stating carefully. A specification is not a document; it is the set of decisions a team must agree on before the work can be done and judged. A prototype is an artefact that behaves — you can click it and watch it respond. The claim is that when building a behaving artefact becomes cheap enough, the artefact becomes the cheapest and most accurate way to communicate a large subset of those decisions, and prose should be reserved for the subset the artefact cannot carry.

The problem this was invented to solve is old. Specification by prose has a well-known failure: language is ambiguous about behaviour. The idea that you should show working software rather than argue about descriptions of it is at least as old as the Agile Manifesto of 2001 ("working software over comprehensive documentation"), and was sharpened by Jeff Patton's user-story mapping and by Marty Cagan's insistence through the 2010s that a prototype is the product manager's most important artefact. What changed after 2023 was cost. A clickable, data-backed prototype that in 2018 required a designer and an engineer for two weeks can now be produced by the product manager alone in a day or two using AI coding tools. When the price of the artefact falls by an order of magnitude, the question stops being "can we afford to prototype?" and becomes "what is the document still for?"

The sentence Meera could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "The prototype specifies what the system does where you can see it; we still have to write down what it does where you cannot."

3. How it actually works: sorting decisions by medium

The mechanism underneath the slogan is a sorting exercise. Every feature requires a set of decisions. Some are observable in a running artefact — you look at it and you know the answer. Others are silent: the artefact either does not exercise them, or answers them accidentally in a way no one notices.

In practice the sorting runs in five steps, two of which practitioners routinely leave implicit. First, build the artefact — this is now the cheap step. Second, inventory the decisions the feature actually requires, which almost nobody does explicitly. Third, walk the prototype and mark each inventoried decision as shown, shown-by-accident, or absent. Fourth, write prose only for the absent and the accidental. Fifth — the step that separates teams that recover from teams that do not — state the artefact's status: is this prototype a picture of the intended product, a proposal, or the actual code that will ship? Rohit's prototype was ambiguous on exactly that point, which is why Kaushik's Slack message was sharp.

"Shown by accident" deserves its own attention. Rohit's prototype sorted the technician queue by distance because that is what the AI assistant produced when he asked for a dispatch list. He had not decided that. If the team builds what they see, Baithak will ship distance-based prioritisation to eleven service networks, three of which have contractually promised customers a two-hour response on premium warranty jobs regardless of distance. An accidental decision made visible is the most dangerous category in the whole practice, because it wears the clothing of an intentional one.

4. A worked example: the decision inventory for auto-dispatch

Meera did the arithmetic on Wednesday morning. She and Rohit listed every decision the auto-dispatch feature required before it could ship — sixty-two in total. They then walked the prototype and classified each.

Baithak's fully loaded cost for an engineer in Pune is about ₹22 lakh a year, which at roughly 2,000 productive hours is ₹1,100 an hour. Historically, when a decision is left silent, 60 per cent of the time it surfaces during the build (cheap), 30 per cent in QA (moderate), and 10 per cent in production (expensive, and occasionally a credit against the SLA).

Take the 21 silent decisions at a blended average of 12 rework hours each when discovered late. Expected rework from leaving all 21 silent: 21 × 12 = 252 hours, or about ₹2.77 lakh, before any SLA penalty. Add the 13 accidental decisions, which cost six hours each to unwind once built: 13 × 6 = 78 hours, ₹0.86 lakh. Total expected waste from shipping the prototype alone as the spec: 330 hours, roughly ₹3.63 lakh, against a feature whose entire build budget was 640 hours.

Now change one input. Suppose Meera adds a four-page written companion — a decision ledger listing the 21 silent decisions with an answer and a reason, plus a limits sheet naming the three non-functional numbers. Writing it costs Rohit six hours plus two hours of Kaushik's review: eight hours, ₹0.09 lakh. Assume it resolves 15 of the 21 silent decisions upfront and converts all 13 accidental ones into deliberate ones at no build cost. The remaining six silent decisions still cost 6 × 12 = 72 hours, ₹0.79 lakh. Total: 80 hours, about ₹0.88 lakh. Eight hours of writing removed roughly 250 hours of rework — a return of about thirty to one.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Fidelity is not specification

A prototype built by an AI assistant looks finished. Rounded corners, real-looking Indian names in the technician list, a working map. Visual fidelity persuades people that decision coverage is equally high; it is not. The two are independent, and AI tooling has pushed fidelity up while leaving coverage where it was. Learn to ask, of any polished artefact, "how many of the required decisions does this actually answer?" rather than "does this look ready?"

Silence reads as agreement

If a prototype never shows what happens when no technician is free, every reviewer walks away assuming their own answer, and each assumes theirs is shared. A prose document that omits the same case at least looks incomplete; a running artefact that omits it looks complete. This asymmetry is the single strongest argument against using a prototype alone.

Non-functional behaviour is invisible by construction

Rohit's prototype ran against 30 seeded jobs on his laptop. Baithak's production load is 4.2 lakh jobs a month with peaks near 900 concurrent dispatches on the Saturday before Diwali. No amount of clicking a prototype tells you whether the assignment query stays under four seconds at that volume. Performance, concurrency, offline tolerance and failure behaviour are the classic non-functional requirements, and they are precisely the ones a demo cannot exercise.

Rationale does not survive in the artefact

A prototype records the choice but not the reason. Six months later, when a customer asks Baithak to prioritise premium-warranty jobs, no one can tell whether distance-based sorting was a considered trade-off or an accident of generation. Rationale is the cheapest thing to write and the most expensive thing to reconstruct.

Prototypes anchor reviewers on the wrong layer

Show a stakeholder a document and they argue about the model. Show them a screen and they argue about the button. Baithak's sales head in New Jersey spent his entire review of Rohit's prototype on the colour of the urgency badge and said nothing about whether auto-dispatch should be allowed to override a dispatcher's manual assignment — a far larger question. Anchoring is a real cost of the medium, not a failure of the audience.

It is routinely confused with three other things

With a design mock (which specifies appearance but has no behaviour); with an engineering spike (built to answer a technical feasibility question and then thrown away); and with a pilot (real code, real users, deliberately limited scope). Each has a different disposal plan and a different standard of evidence. The most expensive confusion is between prototype and pilot: code written to demonstrate is not code written to operate, and quietly promoting one to the other is how teams acquire six months of invisible debt.

What it cannot tell you however well you apply it

A prototype tells you whether something can be built and how it feels. It does not tell you whether anyone wants it. Enthusiasm in a demo is a notoriously weak signal of purchase or of sustained use — people are polite about artefacts that a colleague clearly worked hard on. Nor can it tell you whether the underlying model or data holds up: an AI-assisted prototype that classifies job urgency correctly on 30 curated examples says almost nothing about its accuracy on 4.2 lakh messy ones.

Questions a thoughtful newcomer should ask before relying on it

Four are sufficient most of the time. What is the decision inventory, and how many items does this artefact actually settle? Whose signature does this need — an engineer's, a regulator's, a procurement officer's — and does the artefact speak that person's language? Is the data in it real, sampled or invented? And what happens to this code on the day the decision is made: deleted, or merged?

6. How the practice shifts by product type and stage

In consumer products, the prototype is at its strongest: the decisions that matter most are the observable ones — flow, friction, feel — and the fastest way to be wrong about them is to describe them in words. A consumer team at an early-stage company can reasonably let the prototype carry eighty per cent of the specification and keep a one-page ledger.

In B2B software like Baithak's, the ratio inverts as the contract grows. The observable surface is a modest part of what the buyer is purchasing; the rest is uptime, audit trails, role-based permissions, data residency, and integration with whatever the customer's existing ERP is. Those decisions live almost entirely in the silent column. A prototype still earns its place — it collapses weeks of argument about the dispatcher's screen — but it cannot be the specification of record when a ₹3.4 crore contract with a four-second SLA sits behind it.

Marketplaces sit in an awkward middle. A prototype can only show one side of the market at a time, and the interesting decisions in a marketplace are about the interaction between sides: what a technician sees when a job is reassigned away from them, what the brand sees when its network is saturated. Teams that prototype marketplaces well build two artefacts and a written description of the coupling between them.

Stage matters as much as type. In a twelve-person company, the person who builds the prototype, writes the ledger and answers the engineer's question is often the same person, and the written residue can be thin because the oral tradition is strong. At a 900-person company, the prototype passes through people who were not in the room: a designer in Berlin, a customer-success lead in Singapore, a data scientist in Toronto who will be asked in March why the model behaves as it does. Written residue is not bureaucracy at that size; it is the only thing that survives the timezone gap.

7. Common mistakes

Shipping the demo

Symptom from outside: the feature reaches production suspiciously fast and then generates a cluster of production incidents in its third week, all of them concurrency or volume related. Underlying misunderstanding: treating generated code as production code because it runs. Cheapest diagnostic: ask what load the artefact has been run against, and ask for the number. If the answer is a shrug or "it works on my machine", the prototype has been promoted without anyone deciding to promote it.

Writing the PRD anyway, afterwards

Symptom: a nine-page document appears after the prototype is approved, and nobody reads it. Misunderstanding: that the document's purpose is completeness rather than coverage of what the artefact missed. Diagnostic: count how many paragraphs of the document describe something visible in the prototype. If it is more than a fifth, the document is transcription, not specification.

Letting the artefact make decisions nobody owns

Symptom: a team argues in month three about a behaviour, and the only justification anyone can produce is "that's how it was in the prototype". Misunderstanding: that generated defaults are choices. Diagnostic: pick three defaults in the artefact and ask the product manager who decided them and why. Two confident answers out of three is healthy; zero is a warning.

Using the prototype as evidence of demand

Symptom: "we showed it to four customers and they loved it" appears in a business case. Misunderstanding: conflating a reaction to an artefact with a commitment to use or pay. Diagnostic: ask what each customer did next — signed a pilot agreement, named a date, nominated a team — rather than what they said.

8. What good looks like

A team handling this well produces a package, not a document or a demo. The package has three parts: the running artefact, with its status stamped on it ("proposal, not production; to be deleted on merge"); a decision ledger of two to five pages covering the silent decisions, each with an answer and a one-line reason; and a limits sheet naming the three to six numbers the system must hold — in Baithak's case four seconds at the 95th percentile, 900 concurrent dispatches, 30-day location retention under the DPDP Act. Review takes ninety minutes with engineering and design in the room, the artefact projected, and the ledger open beside it. The ledger is amended live. Nobody writes a nine-page PRD, and nobody pretends the demo settled everything.

9. What Meera decided

On Thursday 16 October, Meera told the team that Rohit's prototype was the specification of record for the dispatcher's interface and for the flow — the 41 visible decisions — and that it would be deleted, not merged, when the build began. She asked Rohit for a four-page ledger by Monday covering the 21 silent decisions, and asked Kaushik to sign off on a limits sheet with three numbers on it. She also made one non-obvious call: she flagged the distance-based sort as an accidental decision and reopened it, which surfaced the premium-warranty conflict three weeks before it would otherwise have reached a customer.

Her reasoning was economic rather than philosophical. Prose and prototypes are both media for transmitting decisions, and the AI shift changed the relative price of one of them dramatically while leaving the other where it was. The right response to a price change is to shift the mix, not to abandon the more expensive input entirely — because the expensive input is still the only one that carries edge cases, limits and reasons.

What to learn next follows directly. First, what a PRD becomes when the reader can build: if the document is no longer the specification, the residual document has a different and smaller job, and knowing its new shape is the practical follow-on. Second, team shape as the PM–design–engineering gap narrows: when a product manager can produce a working artefact, the boundaries of the three roles move, and the question of who owns which decisions has to be re-answered.

Two questions to sit with.

1. Take a feature your team shipped in the last quarter. How many of its decisions would a prototype have made visible, and how many were settled in a conversation nobody recorded? What did the unrecorded ones cost?

2. If a prototype cannot demonstrate demand, and a document cannot demonstrate feel, what is the third artefact your team needs — and who in your organisation would be responsible for producing it?

AI & Data Products › How AI Is Changing PM Practice

The prototype as the new specification

A working artefact is a nearly perfect transmission medium for the decisions you can see, and a nearly useless one for the decisions you cannot. Command of this topic means knowing the ratio, in your product, before you choose the medium.

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On the morning of Tuesday 3 February 2026, Ishaan Fernandes, head of product at Rehnuma Care in Lower Parel, Mumbai, was looking at three versions of the same thing. Rehnuma is a consumer chronic-care company: an app that coaches roughly 18 lakh monthly active users through diabetes and hypertension management, sells quarterly coaching plans at ₹1,499, and routes lab tests through partner diagnostics chains. It competes for attention with Tata 1mg, Apollo 24|7, Practo and HealthifyMe, and its retention curve is its entire business — a subscriber who lapses in month two costs the company its acquisition spend of about ₹900.

The three versions were three onboarding flows for a new AI coaching feature, all built the previous week by two product managers and a designer using AI coding tools. Each ran. Each pulled from a seeded database of 40 fictional patients. Each took under a day to produce. Lena Brandt, the designer, working from Berlin, had sent a message at what was midnight her time: "We have three answers and no question. Which decision are these three prototypes trying to settle?" Ishaan had until Friday to hand something to engineering, because the build window closed before the team's April release train.

Eight days later and 150 kilometres away, on Wednesday 11 February, Vikram Salvi faced a decision that looked superficially similar and was structurally different. Vikram is VP Product at Sthapak Build Cloud in Baner, Pune, which sells procurement and site-materials software to mid-sized construction and infrastructure firms — the sort of company that builds a 400-flat township in Nagpur or a logistics park outside Chennai. Sthapak has 61 customers, an average contract value of ₹34 lakh, a product that must produce GST-compliant e-invoices, and a two-year-old integration with SAP that no one wants to touch. Its largest account, a developer group in Dubai, contributes ₹2.9 crore a year and has a written acceptance-criteria annexe in its contract.

Sthapak's problem was that a prototype of a new multi-level purchase-approval matrix, built by a product manager in nine hours, had been shown by the sales head in New Jersey to that Dubai client on a Thursday call. The client's procurement director had replied, in writing, "this is what we signed up for." Nobody at Sthapak had decided that the prototype was a commitment. The artefact had made the decision on the organisation's behalf.

Both companies had discovered the same thing from opposite ends: when producing a behaving artefact costs a day, the artefact stops being a step in the process and starts being the process — including the parts of the process nobody intended to delegate to it.

2. The idea, its history, and the four schools that disagree about it

Begin with definitions, because the loose vocabulary here does real damage. A specification is the set of decisions that must be settled and shared before work can be built and judged; it is a set, not a document. A prototype is an artefact that behaves under interaction. A mock looks but does not behave. A spike is code written to answer a technical question and then discarded. A pilot is production code deliberately limited in scope. The proposition under examination is: when the marginal cost of producing a behaving artefact collapses, the artefact becomes the cheapest high-fidelity carrier for a substantial subset of specification decisions, and written prose should be repositioned to carry only the complement.

The intellectual history is longer than the current enthusiasm suggests. Fred Brooks, in The Mythical Man-Month (1975), advised planning to throw one away, and in "No Silver Bullet" (1986) named the central difficulty: the hardest single part of building a software system is deciding precisely what to build, and no amount of written description substitutes for iterating with users on something that runs. Barry Boehm's spiral model (1988) made prototyping a formal risk-reduction step rather than an informal courtesy. The Agile Manifesto (2001) put "working software over comprehensive documentation" into circulation, with the crucial and usually dropped qualifier that the right-hand item still has value. Gojko Adzic's Specification by Example (2011) and the behaviour-driven-development tradition made the executable test, not the screen, the carrier of the contract. Marty Cagan spent the 2010s arguing that the prototype is the product manager's primary artefact. Basecamp's Shape Up (2019) pushed hard in the other direction: specify at the level of "breadboards" and "fat marker sketches", because high-fidelity artefacts over-specify and rob engineers of the design space where the good solutions live.

What changed between 2023 and 2026 was not the argument but the price. A behaving, data-backed artefact that in 2018 consumed a designer and an engineer for a fortnight can now be produced by a product manager in nine to eleven hours. That is roughly a twentyfold reduction in cost and a fiftyfold reduction in calendar time. Economic logic says a price collapse of that size should shift the input mix substantially, and it has. It does not say the mix should go to a corner solution.

The artefact-first position is overwhelmingly right for Rehnuma's onboarding flow and close to irrelevant for the conformance annexe in Sthapak's Dubai contract. The productive question is never "which school is correct" but "which decisions am I transmitting, to whom, and what will they do with the transmission."

3. Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic

Expert practice reduces to four operations: inventory, coverage assessment, medium assignment, and status declaration. Only the first is laborious, and it is the one most teams skip.

Inventory. Enumerate the decisions the feature requires. Rehnuma's AI coaching onboarding produced 74; Sthapak's approval matrix produced 118, the difference being almost entirely permissions, audit, integration and contractual items. An inventory is not a task list; it is a list of questions to which a wrong answer would produce rework or harm.

Coverage. For each decision, classify how the candidate artefact answers it: shown (a reviewer will read the answer correctly), shown accidentally (the artefact displays an answer nobody chose), or absent. The coverage ratio is the share of decisions in the first category.

Medium assignment and the arithmetic. A formal treatment exists and is worth doing once, properly, because it explains why the answer is a mixture. Let each decision d have a cost c(d) if it is transmitted wrongly and discovered late. Let f(m, d) be the probability that medium m transmits d correctly. The expected waste of a communication plan is Σd (1 − f(md, d)) · c(d).

Rehnuma's own post-mortem data over four releases gives usable numbers. For visible decisions, a running artefact transmits correctly about 96 per cent of the time; careful prose transmits the same decisions correctly about 70 per cent of the time, because readers substitute their own picture. For invisible decisions, an artefact transmits correctly about 5 per cent of the time — essentially the rate at which someone happens to ask the right question during a demo — while written prose transmits correctly about 85 per cent of the time when the decision has actually been made and written.

Apply this to Rehnuma's 74 decisions. Assume visible decisions cost 4 engineer-hours each to unwind late, and invisible ones 18, at a fully loaded ₹1,400 per hour for a Mumbai engineer. Prototype alone: visible waste = 50 × 0.04 × 4 = 8 hours; invisible waste = 24 × 0.95 × 18 = 410 hours; total 418 hours, about ₹5.85 lakh. Prose alone: visible = 50 × 0.30 × 4 = 60 hours; invisible = 24 × 0.15 × 18 = 65 hours; total 125 hours, ₹1.75 lakh, plus roughly seven working days of calendar. The mixture — artefact for the visible fifty, a written ledger for the absent twenty-four — gives 8 + 65 = 73 hours, about ₹1.02 lakh, and costs six hours to produce.

The same arithmetic at Sthapak gives a different verdict, and this is the point. With 50 visible and 68 invisible decisions, and invisible decisions costing far more — a mis-specified delegation-of-authority limit in the Dubai contract is not an 18-hour problem but a 200-hour problem with a commercial tail — prototype alone yields roughly 68 × 0.95 × 200 = 12,920 hours of expected waste in the extreme reading. Even discounting heavily for the fact that senior engineers ask good questions in demos, the structural conclusion holds: at Sthapak the written complement is not a supplement to the artefact, it is the larger half of the specification.

Status declaration. The fourth operation is the one Sthapak omitted. Every artefact needs three properties stamped on it: what it claims (proposal, agreed specification, or shipped behaviour), who may show it outside the team, and what happens to the code on the day the decision is made. Sthapak had no policy on the second, which is how a nine-hour prototype became a written commercial expectation in Dubai.

Second-order effects experts watch for

Three effects appear only after a team has been working this way for a quarter or two. The first is attention reallocation. A running artefact pulls reviewer attention to the pixel layer. At Rehnuma, an analysis of comments on three prototype reviews found 61 per cent concerned typography, colour and copy, 22 per cent flow, and 17 per cent model or policy questions. The same reviewers, given a written proposal the previous quarter, split roughly 15/30/55. The artefact did not make the reviewers shallower; it made shallow comments cheaper to produce.

The second is generated-default drift. AI coding tools carry priors from their training distribution, which is overwhelmingly American. Rehnuma's first generated onboarding had a "First name / Last name" pair, MM/DD/YYYY dates, a "ZIP code" field and a dollar sign on the plan price. Those are four product decisions the model made, none of which anyone chose, all of which are wrong for an Indian consumer health app where a single-field name and a six-digit PIN code are correct and ₹ is not optional. The dangerous ones are subtler: a default that assumes one user per account, in a market where a family shares a phone, or an address form that cannot express "opposite the Hanuman temple".

The third is prototype inflation. When everyone can build, the number of artefacts per decision rises faster than the organisation's capacity to review them. Ishaan's Monday problem was not that he had no artefact; it was that he had three, none of which was tied to a stated question, and a review calendar that could hold one proper ninety-minute session that week. Review capacity, not build capacity, became the binding constraint — a pattern worth recognising because it recurs everywhere AI lowers production cost.

4. When the practice applies, stated as testable claims

An expert converts the fashion into five conditions that can be checked in an afternoon.

There is a category where the idea is not merely inapplicable but actively misleading: any product whose value sits in a property the artefact cannot express. Latency under load, model accuracy on the tail, cost per inference, failure behaviour, and correctness of money arithmetic all belong here. A prototype of a payments reconciliation screen is a beautiful picture of the easy half of a hard problem, and the better it looks the more confidently the organisation will under-resource the other half.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the organisational seams

Multi-product companies. A prototype generated in isolation will violate invariants that exist across the suite — a navigation pattern, a permissions model, a notification budget. The artefact makes local decisions with global consequences, and because it looks finished, the violation is discovered at integration rather than at design. Mature multi-product firms handle this by generating prototypes against a constrained component library rather than from scratch, which lowers fidelity slightly and raises truthfulness considerably.

Two-sided products. A marketplace prototype shows one side at a time. The decisions that determine whether a marketplace works — what the supply side sees when demand is reallocated away from it, how a rating propagates, what happens in a thin market at 11 p.m. in Indore — are decisions about the coupling between the sides. They are invisible in any single-side artefact by construction, and no amount of fidelity fixes it.

Regulated products. In anything touching RBI, SEBI or IRDAI supervision, or the DPDP Act's consent and retention obligations, the regulator's unit of account is an enumerable requirement with an owner and a trace to evidence. A demonstration cannot discharge that obligation. The sophisticated move is not to abandon prototyping but to separate the two artefacts explicitly: the prototype settles the experience, and a requirements register — often maintained by compliance, not product — settles what must be provable.

Hardware plus software. An electric-two-wheeler company on the Ather or Ola Electric model cannot let a software prototype carry the specification past the point where tooling is committed, because the physical world has a spec-freeze date that software does not. The prototype also cannot represent thermal limits, battery-state uncertainty, or what the interface must do when the vehicle is moving at 45 km/h in Bengaluru traffic and the rider has gloves on.

AI-native features. This is the sharpest case and the most current. An AI feature's behaviour is a distribution, not a function. A demo is a sample — usually a sample the demonstrator selected, consciously or not, for being good. Rehnuma's AI coach performed beautifully across the twenty conversations Ishaan had run. On a 1,200-conversation eval set assembled later by Aditi Sundaram, the data scientist in Toronto, it produced advice a clinician flagged as unsafe in 11 per cent of cases involving insulin dosing, and hallucinated a non-existent drug interaction twice. For AI features, the specification of record is the eval suite plus its pass thresholds; the prototype specifies the surface only.

What mature companies say and what they do diverge here in a recognisable way. Large Indian product organisations — the Freshworks and Zoho generation of enterprise software, and the larger consumer platforms — will say in public that they are artefact-first and that documents are dead. Inside, a tech lead writes a technical design document that becomes the real specification of record, and the prototype functions as an input to it. That arrangement works well and is honest about the division of labour; it goes wrong only when nobody admits the design document exists, so product managers stop reading it and discover in month four that a decision they thought they had made was quietly re-made by someone reasonable.

6. Ten nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Coverage and fidelity are independent, and AI moved only one of them

The obvious reading is that a better-looking prototype specifies more. It does not; it specifies the same decisions more persuasively. Tell-tale sign: a review in which every comment is about spacing, tone and colour, and the meeting ends on time. Genuine coverage produces uncomfortable questions and overruns.

Silence is read as consent, and artefacts are silent differently from documents

An incomplete document looks incomplete; an incomplete artefact looks complete. This asymmetry is the deepest argument in the whole topic. Tell-tale sign: the phrase "we assumed" appearing three or more times in a single sprint review, each time about a different assumption, each held confidently by a different person.

A demo of a stochastic system is a sample of size one

When the feature is AI-powered, the artefact you show is one draw from a distribution whose variance you have not measured. The obvious reading — "I've tried it twenty times and it's good" — confuses a mean with a tail. Tell-tale sign: the same three inputs are used in every demo. Experts ask to type their own input, in Hinglish, with a typo.

Generated defaults are decisions with an author who is not in the room

Every default in a generated artefact came from somewhere, and that somewhere is a training distribution. Tell-tale sign: American conventions surviving into an Indian product — ZIP codes, MM/DD dates, two-part names, imperial units — which tells you nobody has audited the defaults, which in turn tells you the subtler ones are also unaudited.

The artefact is a commitment device the moment it leaves the team

Internally a prototype is a question. Externally it is a promise, because the recipient has no way to distinguish a proposal from a preview. Tell-tale sign: a salesperson asking for "the link" rather than the deck. The correct response is not refusal but an explicit status stamp and a rule about who may demonstrate what.

The disposal plan is the specification decision nobody writes down

Whether generated code is deleted at build start or merged into the product determines its standard of quality, its security review, its test coverage and its licence obligations. Teams that do not decide this decide it by default, and the default is "merged, untested, unreviewed". Tell-tale sign: ask three people whether the prototype ships; count distinct answers.

Review capacity is the new bottleneck, and it is inelastic

Build capacity rose twentyfold; the number of hours a senior engineer and a designer can spend attending carefully to an artefact did not change at all. Tell-tale sign: more artefacts than review slots, with the queue resolved by seniority or volume rather than by which decision is most consequential.

Negative space is never in the artefact

What the system must not do — must not auto-approve above ₹50 lakh, must not send a notification after 9 p.m., must not store technician location beyond thirty days — cannot be demonstrated. Tell-tale sign: no "out of scope" or "must not" list anywhere in the package. Its absence is almost diagnostic of prototype-only specification.

Rationale decays faster than the artefact

A prototype records what was chosen and never why. Six months later the reasoning is unrecoverable, and the team cannot tell a deliberate trade-off from a generated accident. Tell-tale sign: "that's how it was in the prototype" offered as a justification in a design discussion.

Feasibility and feel are not demand

The most experienced practitioners are the most careful here. A prototype is strong evidence about whether something can exist and how it feels; it is weak evidence about whether anyone will pay or persist. Tell-tale sign: customer reactions to a demo cited in a business case, with no subsequent behaviour — a signed pilot, a nominated team, a date — recorded alongside them.

7. Variation by product type and company stage

In consumer products, the observable share of the inventory is typically 55 to 70 per cent, and the cost of a wrong observable decision is high because it shows up in retention within weeks. The artefact deserves to carry most of the specification. In B2B and enterprise software, the observable share falls to 25 to 40 per cent, and the invisible decisions carry contractual and audit consequences; the written complement is the bigger half. In platforms and marketplaces, single-side artefacts systematically flatter the design, and the honest practice is two artefacts plus a written description of the coupling. In hardware, the practice is bounded by physical freeze dates and by properties no screen can express. In AI products, the specification bifurcates: the surface goes in the artefact, the behaviour goes in the eval suite, and confusing the two is the characteristic error of 2025 and 2026.

Stage changes the practice less than people expect, and it is worth saying plainly where the difference is not real. The discipline of the status stamp and the disposal plan is identical at twelve people and at twelve hundred; small teams simply get away with omitting it for longer because everyone was in the room. What genuinely changes is the written residue required. At a seed-stage company the oral tradition is strong enough that a one-page ledger suffices. At Sthapak's size — 61 accounts, a Dubai contract, an integration nobody wants to touch — the residue must survive people leaving, which is a different engineering problem entirely. What also changes is the audience: at scale the artefact reaches a designer in Berlin, a customer-success lead in Singapore and a sales head in New Jersey, none of whom were present when the choices were made, and each of whom will read confidence into the polish.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Example A — Rehnuma Care onboarding: the practice working

Ishaan picked one of the three prototypes on Thursday 5 February after doing the thing Lena had asked for: writing down the question. The question was whether the AI coach should be introduced before or after the user enters their first glucose reading. He instrumented both variants as a two-week experiment rather than debating them. Cost of the artefacts: 26 product-manager hours, about ₹58,000 fully loaded. Cost of the ledger covering the 24 absent decisions: 7 hours. Result: coach-first onboarding produced a 4.1-point improvement in day-14 retention on 21,400 new users, worth roughly ₹31 lakh in annualised subscription value at Rehnuma's ₹1,499 price and observed renewal rate. The artefact carried the specification well because the decision was observable and the population was large.

Example B — Sthapak's approval matrix: the practice failing

The Dubai episode cost Sthapak fourteen weeks. The prototype showed a five-level approval chain with a clean visual escalation. What it did not show, because the seeded data contained no such case, was what happens when an approver is on leave during Diwali and a ₹2.4 crore steel order needs releasing within the price-validity window of the quote. Nor did it show the UAE VAT variant, nor the fact that the client's own delegation-of-authority policy required dual approval above AED 500,000 with a documented audit trail.

Once the client's procurement director had written "this is what we signed up for", Sthapak was negotiating from a position it had never chosen. The recovery was not technical. Vikram's team produced a conformance annexe — 68 numbered requirements with owners, derived by walking the prototype and interrogating what it did not show — and took it to the client with an honest account of which of the 68 the demonstration had actually covered (31) and which it had not (37). Nineteen of the 37 became a change order worth ₹46 lakh; the rest were absorbed. Direct engineering cost of the fourteen weeks: about ₹1.9 crore in loaded team cost and deferred roadmap. Sthapak's durable change was mundane and effective: a watermark and a one-line status banner on every prototype, and a rule that nothing without an "agreed specification" stamp may be shown outside the company.

Example C — Rehnuma's AI coach: the specification moving to the eval suite

Aditi's 1,200-conversation evaluation changed the shape of the specification rather than its content. The screens remained exactly as prototyped. What was added was a written pass threshold: zero tolerance for insulin-dosing advice, a required refusal-and-escalate behaviour on 100 per cent of a 90-case safety subset, a ceiling of ₹0.18 per conversation against an observed ₹0.41 in the prototype configuration, and a p95 response latency of 2.5 seconds. Meeting the cost ceiling took a change of model tier and a retrieval step, which changed nothing visible and everything that mattered. The prototype had been a complete specification of a surface and a near-empty specification of a product.

That is not a coincidence: the characteristic weakness of artefact-led specification is that it produces confident impressions, and the only reliable antidote is a question whose answer must be a number, a name or a date.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Position one: the artefact-first maximalists. Their strongest form is not "documents are dead" but "documents are a lossy encoding of an artefact, and now that the artefact is cheap, encoding and decoding are pure waste." The evidence is real: teams that switched report decision cycles shortening from weeks to days, and the 96-versus-70 per cent transmission gap on visible decisions is measurable in any team that keeps post-mortem data. For this position to be wrong, it would have to be the case that the invisible decisions dominate either in number or in cost — which is exactly what Sthapak's inventory shows, and exactly what Rehnuma's does not.

Position two: the executable-specification school. Steelmanned, the claim is that screens are the least durable artefact in software: they change weekly, they encode no invariants, and they do not fail when the system drifts. A test suite or an eval suite is the only specification that defends itself. The evidence is the observed half-life of design decisions versus test assertions. For this to be wrong, it would have to be the case that most of the decisions that matter are not expressible as assertions — which is arguably true for aesthetics, tone and feel, the very decisions where the artefact-first school is strongest. The two positions are, on inspection, describing different halves of the inventory, and yet their adherents genuinely fight, because they disagree about which half is larger in the average product.

Position three: deliberate low fidelity. The Shape Up argument is not laziness; it is a claim about who should be doing the designing. A high-fidelity artefact from a product manager arrives at an engineer as a set of constraints, and the engineer's knowledge of what is cheap and what is expensive never enters the design. Fidelity, on this view, transfers design authority to whoever holds the generation tool, which since 2024 is the product manager — a transfer nobody explicitly approved. For this to be wrong, it would have to be the case that engineers retain real latitude despite the artefact, which depends entirely on the team's culture and on the status stamp being believed.

Position four: writing is a thinking technology, not a transmission technology. This is the strongest and least-discussed objection. The Amazon narrative-memo tradition holds that the value of the six-pager is not that the reader receives it accurately but that the author is forced to think; ambiguity that survives in prose is ambiguity the author had not resolved. On this view, replacing the document with a prototype does not merely change the channel — it removes the discipline that produced clarity in the first place, and AI generation makes this worse, because an artefact can be produced without its author having formed a view at all. For this to be wrong, it would have to be true that building a thing forces as much clarity as writing about it. Ishaan's three unmotivated prototypes are a data point against; a product manager who cannot state the question their artefact answers has not thought, and the tool did not make them.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives at a review with an impressive artefact. Someone who has internalised it arrives with an artefact, a one-page list of the decisions it does not settle, and a stated question the artefact exists to answer. They open by saying what the artefact is not. They ask reviewers to type their own inputs. They know their product's coverage ratio to within ten points without recalculating it. They treat the disposal plan as a decision rather than a detail, and they can tell you, for any default in the artefact, whether a human chose it. When they see a colleague's beautiful generated screen, their first question is about the data behind it and their second is about who has seen it.

Most tellingly, they are medium-agnostic under pressure. Asked to defend prose, they will; asked to defend the artefact, they will. What they will not do is answer the question "should I write the spec or build the thing?" without first asking what the product is and who is going to read the answer.

12. What the two protagonists decided

Ishaan shipped the prototype as the specification of record for the onboarding surface, with a seven-page written ledger covering the 24 absent decisions, and moved the AI coach's specification entirely into Aditi's eval suite with written thresholds. He deleted the three prototypes at build start and said so in writing. His reasoning was that his coverage ratio was high, his audience was internal, and his riskiest decisions were behavioural rather than visual.

Vikram did the opposite in structure and the same in spirit. He kept prototyping — it had shortened Sthapak's design arguments considerably — but declared that at Sthapak the prototype is an input to a written specification, never the specification itself, and instituted the status stamp. His reasoning was that 58 per cent of his decisions were invisible, several were contractual, and the seam between product and sales had already demonstrated that an unstamped artefact will acquire a meaning of its own.

Discussion questions.

1. Estimate the coverage ratio of your own current product area. What evidence would change your estimate by ten points, and why have you not gathered it?

2. Sthapak's fourteen-week loss is usually diagnosed as a sales-process failure. Argue instead that it was a specification failure, and then argue that the distinction is meaningless. Which argument do you find more useful, and for what purpose?

3. If writing is primarily a thinking technology rather than a transmission technology, what should replace it now that artefacts are cheap — and is any team you know of actually doing that?

13. Going deeper

AI-generated prototypes — the enabling capability underneath this entire topic; understanding what these tools do well and badly tells you which parts of an artefact to trust.

AI product design choices — generated design artefacts blur the line between a mock and a product, which is the mechanism behind the status-stamp problem.

When building gets cheap and deciding does not — the economic frame that explains why the artefact replaced the document, and why the shift stops where it does.

What a PRD becomes when the reader can build — the direct successor question: if the artefact carries the visible decisions, what shape does the residual document take?

Team shape as the PM–design–engineering gap narrows — who owns which decisions once a product manager can produce behaving software.

Discovery when synthesis is cheap but evidence isn't — the counterweight to the demand blind spot: a prototype proves feasibility, never desire.

Reviewing work you did not write — the discipline that becomes binding once review capacity, not build capacity, is the bottleneck.

Velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved — a general treatment of the prototype-inflation effect described in section 3.

Taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill — when every artefact looks finished, choosing among them is the remaining hard part.

Analytics when anyone can query the data — the same cheap-production dynamic in a different medium, with the same coverage-versus-fidelity trap.

Products whose marginal cost is no longer near zero — why the ₹0.41-per-conversation number in Example C is a product decision and not an infrastructure detail.

Prayaan Mobility Systems: what the demo promised

Pune, March 2026. Eleven weeks after a three-day prototype was shown on a stage in Delhi, the company must decide what it is actually building — and discover, in the process, who decided.

1. Sunday night, Baner

Meghana Joshi had been awake since four. It was now 11.40 p.m. on Sunday 8 March 2026, the flat in Baner was quiet, and the Pune air had that dry warmth that arrives in the second week of March and never leaves until the rains. On her screen were two documents that could not both be true: a nine-week engineering estimate from Bengaluru and a twenty-two-week estimate from Pune, for what everyone in the company referred to as "the same feature".

On Monday morning at 10.30 she had to give Prayaan Mobility Systems' leadership team the FY27 Q1 commitment. On the 16th she had to present the same commitment to the board, which now included a director from the fund that had led the ₹210 crore Series B in 2024 and had begun asking, politely and repeatedly, when Range Guard would start showing up in revenue.

Range Guard had been demonstrated on a stage at the Bharat Mobility Global Expo in Delhi on 19 January. It had worked beautifully. Nobody in the room had asked what data it ran on.

2. The company, and the decision that still constrains it

Prayaan Mobility Systems was founded in Pune in 2019 by two engineers who had spent four years building telematics for commercial vehicles and had watched India's electric two- and three-wheeler fleets grow from a curiosity into a category. Prayaan sells Fleet OS: a rider app, an operations console, and a battery-and-charging planner used by companies that run delivery and ride-hailing fleets of electric two-wheelers. Its customers are not the household names but the operators behind them — the companies that lease riders and vehicles to quick-commerce and food-delivery platforms, and that live or die on cost per delivery.

By March 2026 Prayaan had 47 customers, about 1.9 lakh vehicles under management, annual recurring revenue of ₹96 crore, and 240 employees: 80 in Pune, 95 in Bengaluru, the rest spread across sales, success and a small design and data group abroad.

The decision that constrains everything today was taken in August 2022. Prayaan had 22 customers and needed a marquee international account. Bawadi Logistics, a Dubai last-mile operator running 9,000 vehicles across the Emirates, was willing to sign — on the condition that Prayaan build zone-based dispatch to match the way Dubai's municipality zones govern delivery routing, and on the condition that the contract carry an acceptance-criteria annexe: 44 numbered requirements, each of which had to be demonstrated before payment milestones released.

Prayaan said yes. To ship in the fifteen weeks available, the Pune team forked the dispatch service. What was meant to be a temporary branch became Prayaan GCC, a separate deployment with its own release train, its own data residency in the UAE, and — four years later — about 31,000 lines of divergence from Prayaan Core. Bawadi now pays ₹7.4 crore a year, is Prayaan's largest single customer at roughly 7.7 per cent of revenue, and its contract comes up for renewal on 30 June 2026. Every feature Prayaan builds must now be built either once and badly, or twice and slowly.

3. The industry around them

India's electric two-wheeler ecosystem in 2026 is crowded and genuinely competitive. Ather Energy and Ola Electric have built their own connected-vehicle stacks; Mahindra's last-mile business supplies three-wheelers to the same fleets Prayaan serves; TVS and Bajaj have electric models in volume. Quick-commerce demand from Zepto, Swiggy Instamart and Blinkit has made rider productivity the operating metric of the entire sector, and the shift from ownership to fleet leasing has created the customer segment Prayaan sells to. Connectivity for the vehicles runs largely over Jio and Airtel IoT SIMs.

Three regulatory and macro facts bear directly on the product. First, AIS-140 telematics standards define what a compliant tracking device must transmit, but say nothing about battery state of charge, which is the OEM's own data and is exposed — or not — through each manufacturer's API on each manufacturer's terms. Second, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act makes continuous rider location a category Prayaan must hold with consent, purpose limitation and a stated retention period; Prayaan's current retention is 180 days and its legal counsel has twice asked why. Third, central and state incentive schemes have pulled fleet purchasing forward in bursts, which means Prayaan's customers add vehicles in lumps of several thousand, usually with three weeks' notice.

Prayaan's exposure is not only Indian. Bawadi is in Dubai. Charmaine Low's team in Singapore supports four operators in Indonesia and the Philippines, where the vehicle mix is different again. And Nikhil Varma, hired in New Jersey in 2025, is trying to open a North American market where the fleets are smaller, the software budgets larger, and the buyers ask for SOC 2 reports before they ask for a demo.

4. What happened, in order

7–9 January 2026. Ira Qureshi, a senior product manager in Bengaluru, spent three days — two of them a weekend — building a working version of an idea she had been arguing for since October: a feature that predicts, mid-shift, whether a rider will run out of charge before completing their assigned orders, and if not, reroutes them through a swap station at the moment that costs the fewest minutes. She used an AI coding assistant, a fortnight of telemetry from a Pune pilot fleet, and Prayaan's existing map service. It ran. It looked finished. She called it Range Guard.

12 January. Ira demonstrated it to Aravind Pillai, Prayaan's CEO, on a video call. The demo ran nine scenarios. All nine were correct. Aravind asked whether it could be shown at the Expo. Ira said yes.

19 January. Aravind demonstrated Range Guard from the stage at the Bharat Mobility Global Expo in Delhi. Two prospects asked for follow-up calls the same afternoon. A trade publication wrote that Prayaan had "launched" predictive range management. Nobody at Prayaan corrected it.

28 January. Nikhil recorded a version of the demo and used it in three North American pitches. In one, he was asked whether Range Guard would be available on the buyer's fleet of Segway and NIU vehicles. He said he would check, and did not.

6 February. Ramez Haddad, head of operations at Bawadi, watched the Expo recording and wrote to his account manager asking when Range Guard would be enabled for Dubai, noting that clause 9.3 of the 2022 contract entitles Bawadi to "continuous product improvements released to the general customer base at no incremental licence fee".

17 February. Sarita Balan's team in Toronto completed an offline evaluation of the prediction model against 62,000 historical shifts drawn from eleven customers. The results are Exhibit 2. They did not match the demo.

24 February. Rajat Deodhar's platform team in Pune produced a data-availability audit, Exhibit 3, which established that the battery state-of-charge telemetry Range Guard depends on is available at the required five-minute granularity for 38 per cent of vehicles under management, and that the Pune pilot fleet Ira had built against was 100 per cent a single OEM with a generous API.

3 March. The two engineering estimates arrived, nine weeks and twenty-two weeks, and did not reconcile. Meghana asked both leads to explain the gap by Friday. On Friday she received two explanations, each internally coherent.

5. The people

Meghana Joshi, VP Product, Pune. Three years at Prayaan, twelve in the industry. Position: the company must commit to something on Monday and she would rather commit to less than to a date she cannot hold. What she is not saying: she approved Ira's Expo demo in a two-line Slack reply without asking what data it ran on, and she knows it.

Aravind Pillai, CEO, Pune. Founder. Position: Range Guard is the differentiator that separates Prayaan from a telematics vendor, and the Q1 commit should include it. Incentive: he is in early conversations about a Series C at a valuation that assumes a software-margin story. What he is not saying: two of the three funds he has spoken to have asked specifically about AI-driven features in production.

Ira Qureshi, Senior Product Manager, Bengaluru. Position: the prototype is the specification; three days produced something that thirty pages would not have, and Prayaan's problem has always been that it writes when it should build. Incentive: Range Guard is hers, and she has been passed over once for a director role. What she is not saying: she knows the pilot fleet was a single OEM, thought it was representative, and has not revisited that assumption in public.

Rajat Deodhar, Platform Engineering Lead, Pune. Fourteen years' experience, owns the telemetry ingestion layer and the GCC fork. Position: twenty-two weeks, because Range Guard in production requires a telemetry normalisation layer across six OEM APIs, backfill for the GCC deployment, and a degraded mode for vehicles with no state-of-charge feed. What he is not saying: he has wanted to rebuild the ingestion layer since 2024, this is the first business case that would fund it, and his team is two engineers short after December's attrition.

Sarita Balan, Head of Data Science, Toronto. Position: the accuracy claim implied by the Expo demo is not supported by the offline evaluation, and nothing should be sold until thresholds are published. What she is not saying: her evaluation covers eleven of 47 customers, over-weights two large Bengaluru fleets, and she has been asking for a dedicated MLOps engineer for three quarters — a fact that colours how she describes the risk.

Annika Sørensen, Design Lead, Berlin. Position: the prototype's rerouting prompt appears mid-ride on the rider's phone, and no one has decided what happens if the rider is moving. Incentive: she has raised rider-safety concerns twice before and been overruled both times, and now documents her objections in writing. What she is not saying: she has asked a contact at a European fleet operator whether this pattern would pass their safety review, informally, which is not something Prayaan authorised.

Nikhil Varma, Head of Sales, North America, New Jersey. Position: Range Guard is the reason three deals are live, and delay costs pipeline. Incentive: his FY27 quota was set assuming the feature. What he is not saying: the largest of the three deals has been slipping for reasons unrelated to Range Guard, and his forecast has counted it in two consecutive quarters.

Charmaine Low, Customer Success Lead, APAC, Singapore. Position: the four South-East Asian accounts have an OEM mix that almost certainly falls outside the 38 per cent, and she would rather not be the one to explain that in June. What she is not saying: one of her accounts has already asked for a pricing concession and she sees Range Guard as leverage she does not want spent elsewhere.

8. The options as Meghana currently frames them

Option A — commit the prototype. Take Bengaluru's nine weeks, ship Range Guard to Class A vehicles in FY27 Q1, and treat Ira's prototype as the specification for everything except the prediction service. This is what Aravind wants and what the pipeline in Exhibit 5 assumes. It leaves Exhibit 3's Classes B, C and D unaddressed, leaves the GCC fork untouched, and leaves Annika's question unowned. It also means the feature will be sold to customers whose fleets it will not fully serve, and Charmaine's four APAC accounts are unlikely to be in Class A.

Option B — commit the platform. Take Rajat's twenty-two weeks, build the telemetry normalisation layer, close the GCC gap, and ship Range Guard to the whole base in FY27 Q2. This makes the feature real everywhere but delivers nothing before Bawadi's 30 June renewal, consumes most of Prayaan's Q1 engineering capacity, and rests on an estimate produced by the person who has wanted to rebuild that layer since 2024.

Option C — reframe the feature. Ship an advisory version that requires no OEM state-of-charge feed at all: the rider reports remaining charge at two points in the shift, and the model predicts from distance, load and historical consumption. It works on 100 per cent of vehicles at lower accuracy, costs perhaps five weeks, and changes what Range Guard is. Ira regards this as a different and worse product. It is also the only option Sarita's 71 per cent number does not directly threaten, because an advisory feature with a visible confidence band makes a different promise.

Meghana had written these three on a page at 9 p.m. Somewhere around 11 she had begun to suspect that the page was the problem. All three options answered the question "what do we build?" and none of them answered the question that had been sitting underneath the week: what exactly did Prayaan commit to on 19 January, and to whom, and who at the company had the authority to make that commitment in nine minutes on a stage in Delhi. She did not know whether that was a question for Monday or a question she was using to avoid Monday.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The Q1 commitment goes to leadership at 10.30 a.m. on Monday 9 March and to the board on 16 March. Engineering capacity for Q1 is 11 engineers in Bengaluru and 9 in Pune, with a headcount freeze in effect until the Series C closes or is abandoned; Rajat's team is already two short. Prayaan has ₹58 crore of cash and 19 months of runway at the current burn.

Bawadi's contract renews on 30 June, carries the 44-requirement acceptance annexe from 2022 and the continuous-improvement clause at 9.3, and represents 7.7 per cent of revenue; the GCC deployment cannot receive a Core release without four weeks of parity work. Rider location data falls under the DPDP Act, and any expansion of telemetry collection requires a revised consent notice through each fleet operator, which historically takes six to eight weeks. Two North American prospects have asked for SOC 2 Type II evidence before contracting. And the nine Expo scenarios, the recording Nikhil used in three pitches, and the trade-press story describing Range Guard as launched are all still in the world, unretracted.

10. Questions for discussion

1. What did Range Guard's prototype actually specify, and what did everyone believe it specified? List the decisions each of the eight people in section 5 believes have been settled.

2. Exhibits 2 and 3 do not contradict each other arithmetically, yet the company has behaved as though only one of them exists. Why? What would have had to happen in January for both to be on the table before the Expo?

3. Exhibits 4, 5 and 6 each contain a number that would change materially under a different and equally defensible method. Identify them, and say which of the three would most change your view of the decision.

4. Whose decision was it that Range Guard would use OEM state-of-charge telemetry — and at what moment was it made? What does your answer imply about how Prayaan should govern artefacts that are built in three days?

5. Annika's rider-safety question has no owner and appears in neither engineering estimate. Is that a process failure, a prioritisation judgement, or evidence that the prototype framed the problem in a way that made the question invisible? Argue the strongest version of each reading.

6. What should Meghana do on Monday morning, and what precisely should she say to the board on the 16th — about Range Guard, about the Expo, and about what Prayaan will and will not commit to for FY27 Q1?

At 11.40 p.m. Meghana had a message from Sarita, time-stamped 1.10 p.m. in Toronto and unread since morning: "Before Monday — can you tell me what decision the 71 per cent is an input to? I can run a different evaluation by Wednesday if I know." Below it, a message from Ira at 10.52 p.m.: "Console screens updated with the Class A scoping. Want me to walk the team through the build tomorrow at 9?" And below that, nothing from Aravind, who had asked on Friday, in a corridor, whether there was any reason this couldn't just go ahead.

She opened the deck, deleted the slide titled Q1 Commitment, and sat looking at the empty space where it had been.

Aalekh Systems: the weekend that became the specification

Hyderabad, November 2025. A product manager builds in eleven hours what the team would have spent three weeks describing. The question is no longer whether to prototype, but what the prototype is allowed to decide.

1. Thursday evening, HITEC City

At 7.15 p.m. on Thursday 20 November 2025, Sneha Ramakrishnan closed her laptop in Aalekh Systems' office on the fourth floor of a glass building off the Cyber Towers junction in Hyderabad, and then opened it again. On Monday morning she had to tell her engineering leads what they would build between the first week of December and the end of March. The February release train was the only window before Aalekh's biggest renewal cycle, and missing it would push the feature into the following financial year.

The feature was called Paathak, and it already existed — after a fashion. Aniket Bhosale, a product manager in Aalekh's Bengaluru office, had built a working version over the Diwali long weekend using an AI coding assistant. It ran in a browser. You dropped a scanned hospital discharge summary into it, and eleven seconds later a claims form appeared, filled in: patient name, admission date, diagnosis code, room category, itemised charges, the lot. Aniket had logged eleven hours of work. Two customers had seen it on video calls and both had asked when they could have it.

Sneha's problem was that nobody at Aalekh had written down what Paathak was supposed to do. They had only built something that did it.

2. Aalekh Systems

Aalekh Systems was founded in 2017 by two former insurance-operations managers who had spent their careers watching claims departments retype information from paper. The company sells Aalekh Claims Desk, a workflow product used by health insurers, third-party administrators and hospital billing departments to move a claim from intake to settlement. It has 34 enterprise customers, annual recurring revenue of ₹41 crore, and a reputation — earned in the unglamorous way — for handling the Indian document reality: a discharge summary might arrive as a clean PDF from a corporate hospital in Gurugram, or as a photograph of a carbon copy taken on a ₹8,000 phone in Warangal, with the doctor's handwriting running across the pharmacy stamp.

The Indian enterprise-software market around Aalekh is crowded and increasingly credible: Freshworks and Zoho have shown that a company headquartered in India can sell globally, Postman has shown that developer trust can be built from Bengaluru, and every large insurer's technology roadmap now has a line item for automation. IRDAI's push towards faster cashless settlement has made claims turnaround a competitive variable rather than a back-office metric. Meanwhile the Digital Personal Data Protection Act has made anything involving patient records a matter of consent, purpose limitation and retention — which in Aalekh's world means that a clever feature with a careless data path is worse than no feature at all.

Aalekh's team is spread thin and wide. Fourteen engineers sit in Bengaluru, six in Pune. Katrin Vogel, the design lead, works from Berlin. Rhea D'Souza, the company's only data scientist, is in Toronto, having moved there in 2023; her overlap with Bengaluru is ninety minutes a day. Wei Lin Tan runs customer success from Singapore, covering the four South-East Asian accounts. Dev Chandrasekhar, head of sales for the Americas, works out of New Jersey. And Rimaal Insurance Services, a Dubai-based health insurer that pays Aalekh ₹2.6 crore a year, is the company's single largest account and its reference customer for the entire Gulf region.

3. The situation

Aniket's prototype had changed the conversation inside Aalekh in four days. Before it existed, Paathak had been an item on a roadmap slide with an estimate of "two quarters" attached. After it existed, everyone had an opinion, and most of the opinions were about the interface.

Dev, in New Jersey, had already shown the prototype on a Tuesday call to a prospect in Chicago. Wei Lin, in Singapore, had asked whether Paathak would handle Bahasa-language documents for the Jakarta account, and had received no answer. Katrin, in Berlin, had written a long message pointing out that the prototype's confidence indicator — a small coloured dot beside each extracted field — implied a precision the system did not have, and that nobody had decided what a claims processor was supposed to do when the dot was amber.

Rhea, in Toronto, had done the thing that made Sneha's decision hard. Over three days she had run Aniket's extraction pipeline against 500 documents pulled at random from the production corpus of two consenting customers, rather than the 40 documents Aniket had used while building. The results were in Exhibit 2, and they were not the results anyone had seen in the demo.

Vivek Nair, who leads the Bengaluru engineering team, had put the matter plainly in a message to Sneha on Wednesday night: "I can build what Aniket has shown me in six weeks. I cannot build what Aalekh is going to be held to in six weeks, and I don't yet know the difference between those two things. Neither, I think, do you."

4. The people

Sneha Ramakrishnan, Director of Product, Hyderabad. Six years at Aalekh, promoted eighteen months ago. She wants the February train and she does not want a repeat of the 2024 auto-adjudication release, which shipped on time and generated eleven customer escalations in its first month.

Aniket Bhosale, Product Manager, Bengaluru. Two years in the role, genuinely gifted with the new tooling. He believes the prototype is the specification, that writing a document about something that already runs is ceremony, and that Aalekh's slowness is its biggest risk. He would like Paathak to be his first significant launch.

Vivek Nair, Engineering Lead, Bengaluru. Twelve years of experience, four at Aalekh. He is not opposed to the prototype; he is opposed to being handed an artefact whose silent decisions become his problem in March. He wants the non-functional numbers written down before he commits a date.

Rhea D'Souza, Data Scientist, Toronto. The only person at Aalekh who has measured anything about Paathak. She wants an evaluation set and published accuracy thresholds before the feature is sold, and is worried that her ninety-minute overlap with Bengaluru means she will hear about decisions after they are made.

Dev Chandrasekhar, Head of Sales, Americas, New Jersey. He has three deals in his pipeline worth ₹5.4 crore in first-year value where automated extraction is the deciding factor. He would like to demonstrate Paathak in January. He does not think of a demonstration as a promise.

5. Exhibits

The three exhibits tell one story. Exhibit 1 shows that the artefact arrived early and cheaply and has already been shown to customers and prospects. Exhibit 2 shows that the property everyone believes they saw — that Paathak reads Indian discharge summaries — was demonstrated on documents chosen by the person demonstrating, and that on a random sample the all-fields-correct rate falls from 90 per cent to 34 per cent. Exhibit 3 shows why that was possible: 31 of the 70 decisions that Paathak requires are visible in the prototype, and the ones that determine whether the feature is safe to sell are not among them.

6. The options

Option A: the prototype is the specification. Hand Aniket's build to Vivek on Monday, ask for a six-week implementation, and let the team resolve the remaining questions as they arise. Upside: the February train is comfortable, Dev gets his January demonstrations, and Aalekh moves at a speed it has never moved at. Cost: the 32 absent decisions get answered by fourteen engineers individually, at build time, without Rhea, Katrin or the compliance review; Aalekh discovers in March what it has promised in January.

Option B: write the full specification first. Three weeks of Sneha's and Aniket's time producing a complete PRD, reviewed by engineering, design, data science and the company's external DPDP counsel, before a line is committed. Upside: nothing silent remains silent. Cost: three of thirteen weeks consumed, the February train becomes tight, and roughly two-thirds of the document will be a prose transcription of things that are already unambiguous in the artefact — the exact ceremony Aniket objects to.

Option C: the artefact plus a written complement. Declare the prototype the specification of record for the 31 visible decisions, and spend one week producing two short written pieces: a decision ledger covering the 32 absent decisions with an answer and a reason for each, and a limits sheet naming the accuracy thresholds, throughput and retention numbers that Paathak must hold. Stamp the prototype with its status, and set a rule about who may demonstrate it externally. Upside: one week, not three; the silent decisions become explicit. Cost: it requires Sneha to make roughly thirty decisions in a week, several of which she would rather defer, and it forces an uncomfortable conversation with Dev about the January demonstrations.

7. Questions for discussion

1. What, precisely, did the two customers who saw Paathak on 4 November agree to? What did Aalekh learn from those demonstrations, and what does it only appear to have learned?

2. Exhibit 2 shows the all-fields-correct rate falling from 90 per cent to 34 per cent. Is this a model problem, a data problem, or a specification problem? What follows from each reading?

3. Using Exhibit 3, which of the 32 absent decisions would you insist on settling before 1 December, and which can safely wait until the build is under way? On what principle are you dividing them?

4. Which option should Sneha take on Monday, and what exactly should she say to Dev in New Jersey about the January demonstrations?

8. A note for the learner

The lens for this case is the idea that a working prototype can carry the specification. The idea is sound and the case does not argue against it — Aniket produced in eleven hours an artefact that settles 31 decisions more precisely than any document would have. The discipline the idea demands is the part Aalekh skipped: knowing which decisions the artefact settles and which it leaves silent, and understanding that a running artefact's silence is read by everyone as agreement, because it looks finished in a way an incomplete document never does.

A well-reasoned answer therefore rejects the framing that the choice is between speed and rigour. Exhibit 3 shows the two media are not substitutes at all: they are cheap for different categories of decision. Prose is a poor way to describe a review screen and an excellent way to record that Paathak must not auto-fill a diagnosis code when its confidence is below the threshold Rhea sets. A strong answer will also notice the accidental decision hiding in the middle row of Exhibit 3: the confidence thresholds behind the coloured dot were produced by the tool, not chosen by anyone, and they are currently the most consequential unowned decision in the product.

One defensible path is Option C, with three specific moves. First, Sneha declares the prototype the specification of record for layout, field order and review flow, and deletes it at build start rather than merging it, so that nobody quietly promotes demonstration code into a DPDP-relevant data path. Second, she spends the week of 24 November producing the ledger and the limits sheet, and gives Rhea the authority to set the accuracy thresholds — including the threshold below which Paathak simply does not offer an answer, which converts Exhibit 2 from a problem into a product decision. Third, she tells Dev that he may demonstrate Paathak in January on the condition that every demonstration opens with the sentence "this is a proposal, not a committed release", and that the deal desk knows no acceptance criteria may reference the demonstration.

The reasoning is economic rather than procedural. One week of writing removes the category of failure that cost Aalekh eleven escalations in 2024, while preserving almost all of the speed the prototype bought. Option A trades a known week for an unknown March; Option B pays three weeks to re-describe things the artefact already says perfectly well. The lesson generalises past this case: when building becomes cheap, the product manager's scarce work is no longer producing the artefact but stating what the artefact does not decide.
